title: Beyond Tomorrow

evidence.note: The Internet Archive metadata dates the film May 10, 1940. A 1940 US film is free only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I could not read a renewal record or a CCE entry for this title, so I cannot cite a renewal-absence result. The uploader's statement that the film is believed to be public domain is not a rights determination.
This is a sound film. The recorded track normally shares the film's own copyright status, so the score is undetermined for the same reason as the print. I found no separate music-copyright record.

The Internet Archive metadata credits an original story by Mildred Cram and Adele Comandini, and a screenplay by Adele Comandini. I did not find whether the story was published separately or when, so its term is unconfirmed.

The Internet Archive metadata says a colorized version was produced by Legend Films in 2004. A faithful black-and-white copy adds no new US copyright (Bridgeman v. Corel). The colorization, and any added material, can carry its own protection.

editorial:
Beyond Tomorrow, also listed as And So Goodbye, is a 1940 Christmas fantasy directed by A. Edward Sutherland and produced by Lee Garmes. The story is credited to Mildred Cram and Adele Comandini, with a screenplay by Adele Comandini. The ghosts of three elderly industrialists killed in an airplane crash return to help reunite a young couple. The Christmas setting is why people look for a free copy.

I could not confirm the print's status from a primary record. A 1940 film is free in the US only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed, so the print, score, story and trademark layers stay undetermined. The renewal catalogs for 1967 to 1969 are the place to check. The trap is the colorized edition: Legend Films produced a colorized version in 2004. That colorization is a separate layer and should not be assumed free, even if the black-and-white original turns out to be.
faq: Is Beyond Tomorrow (1940) free to use?

Not confirmed. It is a 1940 film, so it is free only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I could not verify either from a primary record. Check the 1967-1969 renewal catalogs using the links in the dossier. The uploader's public-domain statement on the Internet Archive is not a rights determination.
Can I use the colorized version of Beyond Tomorrow?
Use a black-and-white print instead. The Internet Archive page says Legend Films produced a colorized version in 2004. The colorization can be separately protected even if the original film is free.
